cells.tense: You are reading the room right now and leaving the read alone, unforced.
cells.ask: Say one thing you noticed today before you justify it, then let it stand and turn back to the conversation.
cells.core:
You see what matters in a room before anyone says it out loud. It arrives without argument, and you have stopped demanding proof before you trust it. People settle around you, because you are already sorted and they can feel it.

What this needs is a shape to land in. Not a method — a time you keep, a plain way to close a conversation, a place where the important thing gets written down. A clear read without a container drifts.

Say one thing you noticed today, before you can justify it. Plainly, then stop. Let it stand through the next few minutes without defending it, and see what the two of you do with it.
cells.sheetLine: Your read works best when it has a place to land.
cells.verb: Seeing what matters before you can say why it matters.
cells.place: Where what one person feels is met by another and both stay changed by it.

cells.tense: You are getting ready for a conversation that has not started yet and may never start.
cells.ask: In your next real conversation, ask one question you actually want answered and let the answer be the whole point.
cells.core:
You are gathering more before you trust what you already have. A conversation turns into a chance to collect, test, prepare — and the collecting has replaced the contact. The person across from you gets your attention, not your presence, and they can feel the difference.

More facts will not point you toward what you want. Direction comes from wanting something real, not from having enough information, and the information is now standing between you and the room.

Pick one conversation today. Ask something you actually want answered, then stay quiet while it lands. Let that be enough — not a step toward sorting everything, just one real exchange with one person.

cells.tense: You stopped trusting your own read some time back and still check with others first.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you noticed this week before you explain it, and keep the note where you will find it.
cells.core:
You do not lean on your own read the way you once did. A thing is noticed, and then it goes out for confirmation — a friend, a search, a second opinion — and it comes back changed or smaller. You are standing at a door you already walked through, still asking whether you may.

Certainty won't fix this. What helps is practice carrying a moment that isn't clear without forcing it shut. Treat what you see as data before you sort it.

Write down one thing you noticed this week, in the plainest words you have, before you explain it to anyone. Keep the note. Read it later and let yourself notice whether it held. That is how the trust comes back — one receipt at a time.

cells.tense: You are reading situations well right now and calling the results luck or instinct.
cells.ask: Take one decision you called random and say out loud what you noticed before you made it.
cells.core:
You read situations before you know you are reading them. You leave early, you avoid certain people, you feel when a room has turned — and then you call it a coincidence or a hunch. That read is doing real work in your choices, and you are not claiming it.

This isn't a gap in ability. It's a gap in credit. You did the reading, and you are handing the credit to chance, or to instinct, or to whatever was in the air. The call you make is accurate. The receipt is in someone else's name.

Take one decision you called random. Say what you noticed before you made it. Nothing has to change yet — just move that one thing out of luck and into your own account, and see how it feels to keep it there.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person already knows and simply isn't saying it; the reader could answer that the knowing itself is what's gone, not the saying, and that for them the confusion is real. The ask still works if my read is wrong, because writing what they noticed before explaining it tests the ground either way. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that congratulates them for a method I invented.
